name: Amazonian & Caribbean
intro: Amazonia and the Caribbean hold two very different bodies of story, and this pack keeps them distinct. In the Amazon basin, Yanomami, Tukanoan and Shipibo-Konibo peoples tell of creators, lawgivers and jaguar-persons whose knowledge is still held by particular families and shamans. In the Greater Antilles, the Taíno peoples told of Yaya, Deminán and the storm power Guabancex; their stories survive mainly through a short account written for Columbus in 1498 and through communities that never disappeared. Both regions were changed by conquest, disease and enslavement, and both are alive. Some knowledge is restricted and is not disclosed here. These retellings are a first draft and need review by Yanomami, Tukanoan, Shipibo-Konibo and Taíno community members before use.

timeline.label: Taíno chiefdoms flourish in the Greater Antilles
timeline.note: Villages and chiefdoms across Ayiti, Borikén and Cuba develop the farming, craft and ceremony that Pané later tried to describe.

timeline.label: Ramón Pané writes his account of Taíno beliefs
timeline.note: A friar living in Ayiti records origin stories for Columbus; his Relación is the main written source and is shaped by its purpose.

timeline.label: Invasion, epidemic disease and enslavement
timeline.note: Spanish conquest and disease kill most of the Taíno population; the record is violent and incomplete, and Taíno people survive it.

timeline.label: The Yurupary cycle is written down
timeline.note: Ermanno Stradelli publishes a long version of the Yurupary story in Italian, based on a nheengatú telling from the Rio Negro.

timeline.label: Amazonian ethnography and its blind spots
timeline.note: Travellers and anthropologists such as Koch-Grünberg, Reichel-Dolmatoff, Hugh-Jones, Turner and Roe record myths and rites, often without community control.

timeline.label: Indigenous testimony and community review
timeline.note: Davi Kopenawa's The Falling Sky (2013), Yanomami land defence and Taíno language and community work put Indigenous voices first; this pack still needs their review.

sources.title: Ramón Pané, Relación acerca de las antigüedades de los indios (c. 1498)
sources.note: The first written account of Taíno religion, compiled on Columbus's orders. It preserves otherwise lost stories but filters them through a friar's purposes and a violent colonial setting.

sources.title: Davi Kopenawa and Bruce Albert, The Falling Sky (2013)
sources.note: A Yanomami shaman's testimony, dictated over years and translated into French and English. It is one telling among many, spoken from a particular community and position.

sources.title: Ermanno Stradelli, La leggenda dell'Jurupary (1890)
sources.note: The earliest long written version of the Yurupary cycle, collected in the Rio Negro region. A foundational but mediated text, and no substitute for Tukanoan knowledge.

sources.title: Stephen Hugh-Jones, The Palm and the Pleiades (1979)
sources.note: A study of initiation and cosmology among the Barasana and neighbouring Tukanoan peoples of the Vaupés, and a key analysis of the Yurupary complex.

sources.title: Jonathan D. Hill, Wakuenai Society (1983) and Keepers of the Sacred Chants (1993)
sources.note: Ethnography and song analysis among Arawakan peoples of the upper Rio Negro, useful on Yurupary, ritual knowledge and its ownership.

sources.title: Peter G. Roe, The Cosmic Zygote (1982)
sources.note: A study of Shipibo cosmology on the Ucayali, including jaguar and water-serpent stories; like all ethnography it is a partial record.

sources.title: Neil L. Whitehead, Dark Shamans (2002)
sources.note: An analysis of Kanaimà and shamanic violence in Amazonia that also examines how colonial violence shaped the written record.
